Candidate errors I did not write for lack of evidence, for a human to promote if a wrong option or caution later supports them. (1) Putting the rate into A = P(1 + in) as a whole number (for example 7.5 or 8) instead of the decimal 0.075 or 0.08. The canonical solution for the question about R500 at 6.85% for 1 year has a slip in its working. It writes i = 0.685 and A = 500(1.685), but 6.85% is 0.0685, so the correct factor is 1.0685. Two questions (R3500 at 6.7% for 4 years, and the R2000 loan at 10% for a year) ask for the interest rather than the accumulated amount. Their canonical solutions find A first and then subtract P. entries.label: Rounds to the nearest year instead of rounding up
entries.description: The student gets a decimal number of years, such as 19.3, and rounds it to the nearest whole number (19) instead of rounding up to the next whole year (20).
entries.signal: The final answer is one year short of the rounded-up value: the decimal from the calculation was below 0.5 and the student rounded it down.

refutation.text_md: You did the hard part right: you rearranged $A = P(1 + in)$, calculated $n$, and got a decimal. Then you rounded it the usual way, to the nearest whole number. That is a good habit for most rounding questions, but it is the wrong rule for this one.

Look at what the decimal means. If $n = 19.3$ years (R1080 growing to R3348 at 10.9% p.a.), the money reaches the goal a little after the 19-year mark. Because $A = P(1 + in)$ gets bigger as $n$ gets bigger, at $n = 19$ the amount is still a little short of R3348.

So rounding down to 19 gives a number of years that does not reach the goal. The answer has to be a whole number of years that does reach it, and the first one that does is $20$. That is why the book's working says to round UP to the nearest year: $19.3$ becomes $20$, not $19$.

Notice that a small decimal part does not change this. The book turns $18.3$ into $19$ years too. Next time, once you have $n$ as a decimal, ask yourself whether that many whole years would reach the goal. If not, go up to the next whole year, whatever the decimal part is.

entries.label: Rounds partway through the calculation
entries.description: The student rounds a working value such as $\frac{A}{P}$ or $\frac{A}{P} - 1$ before finishing, so the final number of years drifts away from the one a full-precision calculation gives.

refutation.text_md: You set it up correctly: divide $A$ by $P$, subtract $1$, then divide by $i$. You rounded the numbers along the way to keep them short. The steps are right. The early rounding is what lets the answer drift.

Each time you round, a little of the true value is thrown away, and that little is carried into the next step. The last step divides by $i$, a small number such as $0.124$. Dividing by $0.124$ is the same as multiplying by about $8$, so a small slip grows to about eight times its size.

This matters most when the answer lands close to a whole number. R6360 growing to R26075 at 12.4% p.a. gives $24.9987\ldots$ years, only about $0.001$ below $25$. With that little room, the number you round up has to be the full-precision one.

Do the whole calculation in one go on the calculator. Type $\left(\frac{A}{P} - 1\right) \div i$ with the real values of $A$, $P$ and $i$, and keep every digit it gives you. Round only at the very end, rounding up to the nearest year.

entries.label: Uses an age, not the time between two ages, as the number of years
entries.description: When a question gives the son's age at the deposit and at the end, the student puts one of those ages into the formula as $n$ instead of the number of years between them.
entries.signal: A rate that is too small (the later age used as $n$) or far too large (the earlier age used as $n$), in a question that gives two ages instead of a number of years.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that the question gives you years, in the form of ages, and you used one of those ages as $n$. That is a natural pick. Your other choices were fine: the formula $A=P(1+in)$ and the values of $A$ and $P$.

The catch is what $n$ counts. It is the number of years the money stayed in the account, not the age on a birthday. The deposit was made at one age and the value was read at a later age, so the money was invested for the difference between the two ages.

Try it on a deposit of R5000 made on a son's fifth birthday that has grown to R18000 by his twenty-first birthday. The money was not in the account at all until he was 5, so it was not invested for 21 years. It was invested for $n=21-5=16$ years.

The difference shows in the answer. With $n=21$, $\dfrac{\left(\frac{18000}{5000}\right)-1}{21}$ is about $0.124$, so about $12.4\%$. With $n=16$ it is $\dfrac{\left(\frac{18000}{5000}\right)-1}{16}=0.1625$, which is $16.25\%$. Spreading the same growth over too many years makes the rate look too small.
So when a question gives two ages, work out $n$ first. Write it with your known values as the later age minus the earlier age, for example $n=21-5=16$, and only then put the numbers into $A=P(1+in)$.

entries.label: Uses the interest charged as $A$
entries.description: When a question gives the interest charged rather than the final value, the student writes that interest as $A$ in $A=P(1+in)$ instead of adding it to the principal first.
entries.signal: A negative rate, because an $A$ smaller than $P$ was put into the formula.

refutation.text_md: You took the interest figure the question gives and used it as $A$. That is easy to do when it is the only amount in the question besides the price. You also had the right principal and the right number of years.
The trouble is what $A$ stands for. In $A=P(1+in)$, $A$ is the value at the end: the original amount together with the interest. The interest figure is only the extra part.

See what happens if you use it. For a purchase of R3750 with R956.25 interest charged over 3 years, $956.25=3750(1+3i)$ gives $\frac{956.25}{3750}=0.255$. Taking 1 away leaves $0.255-1$, which is negative, so $i$ comes out as about $-0.248$. A negative rate would mean the money shrinks, yet interest was added. That tells you $A$ must be bigger than $P$, so something is missing.
What is missing is the principal. The total paid is the principal plus the interest: $3750+956.25=4706.25$. This is $A$.

Now rearrange as usual: $4706.25=3750(1+3i)$, so $1.255=1+3i$, then $0.255=3i$, and $i=0.085$, which is $8.5\%$. Whenever a question gives interest instead of a final value, add it to $P$ first to get $A$.

entries.label: Divides by $n$ without first taking away the 1
entries.description: After reaching $\frac{A}{P}=1+in$, the student divides $\frac{A}{P}$ by $n$ straight away, so the 1 never gets removed.
entries.signal: A rate that is much too large, equal to $\frac{A}{P}\div n$ written as a percentage, for example 32 where the correct answer is 12.

refutation.text_md: You reached $\frac{A}{P}=1+in$ correctly, and dividing by $n$ is the right idea. The slip is doing it too early: the 1 sits beside $in$ in the bracket, so $\frac{A}{P}$ divided by $n$ is not $i$.

Test it on R2500 growing to R4000 in 5 years. $\frac{4000}{2500}=1.6$, and $1.6\div5=0.32$, which would be $32\%$. Put $i=0.32$ back into $A=P(1+in)$ and you get $2500(1+0.32\times5)=6500$, not 4000. So that rate is wrong.
Dividing by $n$ only works on $in$, where $i$ is multiplied by $n$. So first take the 1 away from both sides: $\frac{4000}{2500}-1=i\times5$, which is $0.6=5i$.
Now only $i$ is multiplied by 5, so divide by 5: $i=\frac{0.6}{5}=0.12$, which is $12\%$ p.a. Check: $2500(1+0.12\times5)=4000$.
Use the same order every time: divide by $P$, take away 1, then divide by $n$, that is $i=\dfrac{\left(\frac{A}{P}\right)-1}{n}$.

entries.label: Rounds the bracket to two decimals before multiplying by the principal
entries.description: The student works out $(1+i)^n$ on its own, rounds it to two decimal places, and only then multiplies by $P$, so the final amount drifts away from the book's.
entries.signal: The set-up and formula are right, but the final amount is a few rand away from the book's answer, with the bracket's power rounded to two decimals along the way.

refutation.text_md: You set up $A=P(1+i)^n$ correctly, then worked out $(1+i)^n$ first and rounded it to two decimal places before multiplying by the principal. That feels sensible, because the final answer has two decimal places. The set-up was right. The rounding came too early.

Take $\text{R}6970$ at $10.2$ % p.a. for $3$ years. Here $i=0.102$, so $(1+0.102)^3=1.338273\ldots$ If you round that to $1.34$, then $6970\times 1.34=\text{R}9339.80$. The book's answer is $\text{R}9327.76$, so rounding early made it $\text{R}12.04$ too big.

The rounded power is only about $0.0017$ away from the true value. But $6970$ multiplies that small gap, so it grows into whole rand. The larger the principal, the bigger the damage. This is why the book says not to round off until you have reached the solution.
Do the whole calculation in one go: $6970(1+0.102)^3$. Keep every digit the calculator gives you, and round to two decimal places only on the very last line. That gives $\text{R}9327.76$.

entries.label: Stops at the rate without asking if it is realistic
entries.description: The student solves for $i$ and writes the percentage, then stops, without comparing it with realistic returns or commenting on whether the money could actually earn that rate.

refutation.text_md: You found the rate by solving for $i$, and that is the hard part. One job is left: a rate only means something if a bank could actually offer it, so the answer needs a comment, not just a number.
The book gives two realistic returns to compare with: a typical savings account gives about $2$ % p.a., and an aggressive investment portfolio gives about $13$ % p.a.

Now look at Charlie's case. He has $\text{R5000}$ and needs $\text{R10000}$ after $2$ years, and the working gives a rate of $41.42$ % p.a. That is far above even the $13$ % of an aggressive portfolio, let alone the $2$ % of a savings account.
So the comment is that it seems unlikely Charlie will be able to invest his money at $41.42$ % p.a. The calculation is fine. What the comparison shows is that the target is hard to reach.
Next time: after $i = \sqrt[n]{\dfrac{A}{P}} - 1$, write the rate as a percentage p.a., put it beside $2$ % and $13$ %, and finish with one sentence saying whether the rate is realistic.

entries.label: Picks the account with the bigger rate
entries.description: The student compares the two interest rates (11% against 10.5%) and picks the account with the larger rate, without working out each accumulated balance, so the simple-interest account looks like the winner.
entries.signal: Chooses the simple-interest account because 11% is bigger than 10.5%, with no balance worked out for either account.

refutation.text_md: You compared the two rates, and you are right that 11% is bigger than 10.5%. The catch is that the two accounts do not pay interest in the same way, so the rate alone cannot tell you which account ends with more money.

Simple interest is calculated on the starting amount only, every year. Compound interest is calculated on the starting amount plus the interest already earned, so each year's interest is a little bigger than the one before. Over several years, that extra interest on interest can make up for a slightly lower rate.

Work out both accumulated balances. For the simple-interest account with $P=\text{1450}$, $i=\text{0.11}$ and $n=3$: $A=P(1+in)=\text{1450}(1+(\text{0.11})(3))=\text{1450}(\text{1.33})=\text{R1928.50}$.
For the compound-interest account with $i=\text{0.105}$: $A=P(1+i)^{n}=\text{1450}(1+\text{0.105})^{3}=\text{R1956.39}$.
The compound account has the lower rate but ends with more money, so the rate on its own would have given the wrong choice.

When you are asked which account leaves you with more, work out each accumulated balance with its own formula, $A=P(1+in)$ for simple interest and $A=P(1+i)^{n}$ for compound interest, and then compare the two amounts, not the rates.

entries.label: Thinks compound interest is the better deal for everyone
entries.description: The student sees that compound interest grows more and concludes it is the better kind of interest whether they are saving or borrowing, forgetting that growth is good for the one earning the interest and costly for the one paying it.

refutation.text_md: You have noticed something true: compound interest does grow faster than simple interest. What still needs checking is who is holding the money, because "grows more" is good news for the person who is paid the interest and bad news for the person who has to pay it.

With compound interest, interest is calculated on the principal and also on the interest earned in earlier periods. For someone investing, that extra interest is money they earn. For someone who borrows, it is extra money they owe: the amount owed grows exponentially, just as an investment does.

Simple interest is calculated on the principal only, not on interest from earlier periods, so a borrower pays less interest with it. Compound interest means more money for the banker, who is receiving the interest.

A concrete case: $\text{R2250}$ left for $\text{20}$ years comes to $\text{R5062.50}$ with simple interest and $\text{R7564.17}$ with compound interest. If that is money you saved, the second amount is the better one. If it were money you owed, the second amount would be the bigger bill.

Before deciding which kind of interest is better, ask whether you are the one earning the interest or the one paying it. If you are investing, or you are the banker, compound interest is better. If you are borrowing, simple interest costs you less.

entries.label: Picks the deal with the smaller monthly payment
entries.description: The student takes the deal with the smaller monthly payment to be the cheaper one and chooses it without working out how much interest each deal charges.

refutation.text_md: You compared the monthly payments, and R175 a month is easier to carry than R350 a month. That much is true. But the question asks which store charges less interest, and the size of one payment cannot tell you that.

Look at how long each payment goes on for. Store A asks R350 for 24 months: $A = 350 \times 24 = 8400$. Store B asks R175 for 48 months: $A = 175 \times 48 = 8400$. Either way you pay R8400 altogether. Store B's payments are only smaller because they are spread over twice as many months.

Interest is the part of that R8400 which is more than the cash price, so interest $= 8400 - P$. Find $P$ for each store from $A = P(1+in)$ with $i = 0.075$. Store A is 24 months, so $n = 2$. Store B is 48 months, so $n = 4$.

Store B has the bigger $n$, so $1 + in$ is bigger. Dividing the same 8400 by a bigger number gives a smaller $P$, and a smaller $P$ leaves more of the 8400 as interest. So store B charges more interest, and store A is the one that charges less.

When you compare deals, work each one through: $A$ = monthly payment $\times$ number of months, then find $P$ from $A = P(1+in)$, then interest $= A - P$. Compare the interest amounts, not the monthly payments.

entries.label: Uses the full cash price as the loan amount
entries.description: The student puts the whole cash price into the formula as $P$, forgetting that the deposit is paid up front and so is never part of the loan.
entries.signal: The accumulated amount or the monthly repayment is too big, and equals the full cash price put through $A = P(1+in)$ with no deposit subtracted first.

refutation.text_md: You started the formula from the cash price, which is the first number the question gives you, and the rest of your method may well be right. The step that is missing is the deposit: it is paid in cash at the start, so that part of the price is never borrowed.

Interest is only charged on what is borrowed. In $A = P(1+in)$, $P$ is the loan amount, so the deposit has to come off first: deposit $=$ cash price $\times$ the deposit as a fraction of 100, and $P = $ cash price $-$ deposit.

Try a screen with a cash price of R2500, a 10% deposit, 7.5% p.a. simple interest and 24 months. The deposit is $2500 \times 0.1 = 250$, so $P = 2500 - 250 = 2250$ and $A = 2250(1 + 0.075 \times 2) = 2587.50$. The monthly payment is $\frac{2587.50}{24} = 107.81$.

Starting from the full R2500 instead gives $A = 2500(1 + 0.075 \times 2) = 2875$, which is about R119.79 a month. That is too much, because it charges interest on the R250 that was already paid in cash.

Before you use the formula, check for a deposit. If there is one, work it out, subtract it, and use the result as $P$. Then find $A = P(1+in)$ and divide $A$ by the number of months. If the question mentions no deposit, there is nothing to subtract and $P$ is the cash price.

entries.label: Uses a power formula instead of the simple interest formula
entries.description: The student raises $1+i$ to the power $n$, so each year's interest is charged on the interest already added, instead of using the simple interest formula $A = P(1+in)$ that hire purchase uses.

refutation.text_md: You raised $1+i$ to the power $n$, so each year's interest was worked out on the interest already added. It is a natural thing to try, but hire purchase is charged at simple interest, so this is not the formula to use.
With simple interest, the interest is always worked out on the original loan amount $P$ only. That is why $n$ is multiplied by $i$ inside the bracket and is not a power: $A = P(1+in)$.

Take a loan of R4760 at 14% p.a. over 24 months, so $n = 2$. The simple interest formula gives $A = 4760(1 + 0.14 \times 2) = 6092.80$. Raising $1.14$ to the power 2 instead gives about R6186.10, which is more than the agreement charges, so every monthly repayment would come out too high.
With $n = 1$ the two methods give the same amount, which is why a one-year agreement can hide the mix-up. It shows up as soon as the agreement runs for two years or more.
For any hire purchase question: turn the months into years for $n$ (months $\div$ 12), use $A = P(1+in)$, then divide $A$ by the number of months.

flags.text: The canonical solution for the two-stores question (ex9-3-8) has an arithmetic slip. It divides 8400 by 2.15 and by 4.3, but $1 + 0.075 \times 2 = 1.15$ and $1 + 0.075 \times 4 = 1.3$. The printed cash prices (3906.98 and 1953.49) and interest amounts (4493.02 and 6446.51) therefore do not follow from the stated formula. Working it through correctly gives about 7304.35 and 6461.54 for the cash prices, and about 1095.65 and 1938.46 for the interest. The final answer, store A, is unchanged. I kept every one of those intermediate numbers out of the refutation and argued only from $n$ and from the common total of 8400, so the entry is true under both the printed and the corrected arithmetic. entries.label: Multiplying where you should divide, or dividing where you should multiply
entries.description: The student applies the exchange rate in the wrong direction: multiplying rands by the rate to find the foreign amount, or dividing a foreign amount by the rate to find the cost in rands.
entries.signal: An amount of a currency worth more than a rand that comes out bigger than the rand amount it came from (for example 106 800 euros from R10 000), or a rand cost that is smaller than the foreign price.

refutation.text_md: You have the right ingredients, an amount and a rate, but the rate has been used the wrong way round: multiplied where the book divides, or divided where it multiplies. Both operations belong to this topic, so it is easy to reach for the wrong one.
A rate such as $\text{€}1=\text{R}9.20$ says what one euro costs in rands. To find a cost in rands from euros, multiply the number of euros by the rate: $200\times 9.20=\text{R}1840$.

Going the other way, from rands to euros, you are asking how many lots of $\text{R}10.68$ fit into your rands. Saba has $\text{R10000}$ and $\text{€}1=\text{R}10.68$, so $x=\frac{10000}{10.68}=936.33$ euros. Multiplying instead gives $106\,800$ euros, far more euros than rands, which cannot be right when one euro costs more than one rand.

The same idea holds when the rate is written the other way round. With $\text{R}1=0.26\text{PEN}$, changing rands to Peruvian sol means multiplying: $25\,000\times 0.26=6500\text{PEN}$. With $1\text{BRL}=1.17\text{PEN}$, changing sol to Brazilian real means dividing: $\frac{4120}{1.17}=3521.37\text{BRL}$.

Next time, look at the rate and find the currency written with $1$ in front of it. Moving out of that currency, multiply by the rate. Moving into that currency, divide by the rate. Then check the size: a currency worth more than a rand gives fewer units than the rands you started with.

entries.label: Using next month's estimated rate instead of today's rate
entries.description: When the purchase is made now, the student converts with the lower rate that is only estimated for next month instead of the current rate.
entries.signal: The rand cost equals the foreign price times the lower, estimated rate (for the £100 iPod, R1200 instead of R1400).

refutation.text_md: You noticed both rates and used the later, lower one, perhaps because it looks like the better deal. The multiplying is fine. The problem is which rate you picked.

The question gives two rates for two different moments. The current rate is what the bank uses today. The lower rate is only an estimate of what might happen in a month, so it tells you about waiting, not about buying now.

Take the iPod that costs $\text{£}100$, with $\text{£}1=\text{R}14$ today. Buying now: $100\times 14=\text{R}1400$. Using the estimated $\text{R}12$ gives $\text{R}1200$, which is what she would pay only if the rate had already dropped. It has not, so she pays $\text{R}1400$.

Next time, before you calculate, ask when the money changes hands. If the question says now, use the current rate and set the estimated rate aside. Then multiply the foreign price by that current rate.

entries.label: Compares the printed numbers without converting
entries.description: The student compares the amounts as they are printed, treating pounds, dollars and rand as if they were the same unit, so the smallest-looking price seems cheapest and the larger-looking tip seems better.
entries.signal: Chooses the UK as the cheapest car (12 200 is the smallest number printed) or Arinda as the better tip (12 is more than 6).

refutation.text_md: It is natural to look at the numbers first: 12 200 is far smaller than 173 400, and 12 is more than 6. Comparing is the right idea. What is missing is that a pound, a dollar and a rand are not the same size of money, so these numbers cannot be put side by side yet.

Try it on the tips. The £6 tip is 6 lots of R14.13, so $6\times 14.13=\text{R}84.78$. The 12 dollars is 12 lots of R7.04, so $12\times 7.04=\text{R}84.48$. Twice as many dollars sounds like more, but each pound is worth R14.13 and each dollar only R7.04, so the tips are almost equal and the pounds tip is 30 cents more.

Now the car. The £12 200 price becomes $12\ 200\times 14.13=\text{R}172\ 386$, which is very close to the R173 400 price in South Africa, so the UK is nowhere near the cheapest. It is the dollar price that is lowest once it is changed into rands, so the USA is the cheapest.
Next time, convert first. Change every amount into rands with cost in rands = cost in the other currency $\times$ exchange rate, and only then compare the rand amounts.

entries.label: Picks the dearest after converting
entries.description: The student changes the amounts into rands but then chooses the largest rand amount when the question asks for the cheapest, which is the smallest.
entries.signal: Names South Africa as the cheapest car: R173 400 is the largest of the three rand amounts.

refutation.text_md: It looks as if you changed the prices into rands, which is exactly the right first move, and then picked the largest of them. The slip is in which end of the list you choose: "cheapest" asks for the smallest rand amount, not the biggest.

In rands, the car in South Africa costs R173 400 and the car in the UK costs $12\ 200\times 14.13=\text{R}172\ 386$. The USA price, once converted, is lower than both. So the South African price is the highest of the three, which makes South Africa the dearest place to buy this car, not the cheapest.

Think of tips from tour groups, all written in rands. The group that tipped the most has the greatest rand amount and the group that tipped the least has the smallest. "Cheapest" goes with the smallest, just as "least" does.

After converting, write the rand amounts in a list and read the question again. If it says cheapest or least, take the smallest rand amount. If it says best, most or greatest, take the biggest. Then name the country or person that amount belongs to.

Nothing in the evidence separates that error from comparing unconverted numbers, so no second entry was written. The last step of the unconverted-amounts entry states the multiplication rule, which also covers the dividing case.

The canonical solution for the car question prints R154400 for 21 900 x 7.04, but the product is R154 176. The final answer (USA is cheapest) is unaffected and the student text never quotes this figure.

The canonical solution for the tips prints 14.31 as the pound rate, but the table says R14.13 and the printed product R84.78 only works with 14.13. The refutation uses 14.13 and the printed result R84.78.
